title: metanoia
summary: These passages portray turning toward God in different settings. Deuteronomy 30 calls Israel to return after scattering; Ezekiel 18 urges people to turn from wrongdoing and live. Mark 1 presents Jesus’ call to repent and believe the good news. Luke 15 pictures a son returning home, and Acts 2 shows hearers responding to Peter’s announcement. The Hebrew-scripture texts provide a background of return and changed direction, while the Gospel and Acts passages give direct New Testament calls and examples.
historical_context: The references include covenant instruction, prophetic exhortation, a Gospel summary of Jesus’ proclamation, a parable, and a scene of public response in Acts. Their forms and settings come from the biblical texts; no lexical history or broader historical reconstruction is supplied.
canonical_context: Deuteronomy and Ezekiel call Israel to turn back and live. Mark links Jesus’ call to repentance with belief in the good news; Luke’s parable dramatizes a return and reception; Acts depicts a response to apostolic preaching. The group connects turning with restoration, but the parable and the direct calls should not be treated as the same kind of statement.
literary_context: Deuteronomy gives covenant instruction, Ezekiel speaks prophetically, Mark summarizes a proclamation, Luke tells a parable, and Acts narrates a public response. The parable illustrates a movement of return but does not function as a dictionary definition. Reading genre and context keeps the examples from being flattened into a single formula.
covenantal_significance: The references connect turning with return to life and restored relationship with God. Deuteronomy and Ezekiel address Israel’s response; Mark and Acts call hearers to respond to the good news; Luke uses a family story to portray return and welcome. The passages support this connection without making every text a technical account of repentance.
canonical_role: This entry gathers calls to turn, a parable of return, and a narrated response to preaching. It helps readers trace a shared theme across different forms while preserving what each passage actually does.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce metanoia to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
